fields.citation: Augsburg Confession, Article III
fields.note: The Augsburg Confession says: "there are two natures, the divine and the human, inseparably enjoined in one Person, one Christ, true God and true man."

sources.label: International Network of Churches, Declaration of Faith

fields.citation: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration, Article VIII
fields.note: The Solid Declaration says the human nature in Christ, glorified and exalted, "did receive... special, high, great, supernatural, inscrutable, ineffable, heavenly prerogatives," and that Christ had this majesty already "when He was conceived in His mother's womb."

fields.citation: Augsburg Confession, Article III
fields.note: The Augsburg Confession says Christ "was crucified, dead, and buried... He also descended into hell, and truly rose again the third day; afterward He ascended into heaven that He might sit on the right hand of the Father."

sources.label: 1 Corinthians 15 as the hinge of Christian hope
International Network of Churches, Declaration of Faith
National Association of Evangelicals, Statement of Faith

fields.citation: Smalcald Articles (1537), Part II, Article 1, "The First and Chief Article"
fields.note: The Smalcald Articles say: "Jesus Christ, our God and Lord, died for our sins, and was raised again for our justification," and that "there is none other name under heaven, given among men whereby we must be saved." Retargeted from Augsburg Confession, Article III, which speaks of Christ as a sacrifice for sin but not in penal terms as directly as this article does.

sources.label: What Did the Cross Achieve? The Logic of Penal Substitution
International Network of Churches, Declaration of Faith
Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths

fields.citation: Book of Concord, Ecumenical Creeds, the Nicene Creed
fields.note: The Nicene Creed as printed in the Book of Concord confesses the Holy Spirit as the one "who proceedeth from the Father and the Son." Retargeted from Augsburg Confession, Article 1, which affirms the Council of Nicaea's Trinitarian doctrine but does not itself quote the creed's wording on the Spirit's procession.

fields.citation: Formula of Concord, Comprehensive Summary, Rule and Norm
fields.note: The Formula says other confessions and the writings of teachers, ancient and modern, stand "as a witness of the truth and as the unanimously received correct understanding of our predecessors," from and according to which, because the Formula is derived from God's Word, "all other writings should be judged and adjusted." Retargeted from "Rule and Norm 2," which is the paragraph naming the three ecumenical creeds, not this one.

sources.label: Institutes of the Christian Religion
sources.citation: John Calvin, Prefatory Address to Francis I, 1536/1559

sources.label: Formula of Concord, Rule and Norm

fields.citation: Augsburg Confession, Article XIV; Article XXVIII
fields.note: Article XIV says no one should teach or administer the sacraments "unless he be regularly called," and Article XXVIII limits a bishop's power to preaching the gospel and administering the sacraments, without mandating any one form of church government — the basis on which some Lutheran bodies retain the historic episcopate and others do not.

fields.citation: Augsburg Confession, Article IX
fields.note: The Augsburg Confession says children are to be baptized "who, being offered to God through Baptism, are received into God's grace," and condemns the Anabaptists who reject infant baptism.

fields.citation: Augsburg Confession, Article IX; Small Catechism, IV
fields.note: The Small Catechism says baptism "works forgiveness of sins, delivers from death and the devil, and gives eternal salvation to all who believe," through "the word of God which is in and with the water, and faith."

fields.citation: Augsburg Confession, Article X; Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration, Article VII
fields.note: The Solid Declaration says the bread and wine "are the true body and blood of Jesus Christ, which are offered and received, not only by the godly, but also by godless Christians," adding that even an unworthy communicant "receives the true Sacrament... just as truly as he who receives... in the most worthy manner."

fields.citation: Luther's Small Catechism, explanation of the First Article of the Apostles' Creed
fields.note: The Small Catechism confesses God as the one who "has made me and all creatures... out of pure, fatherly, divine goodness and mercy, without any merit or worthiness in me." The catechism affirms God as maker of all things without spelling out creation from nothing as such.

fields.citation: Augsburg Confession, Article III
fields.note: The Augsburg Confession confesses that Christ "was crucified, dead, and buried... and truly rose again the third day," and the Nicene Creed printed in the Book of Concord confesses these events "according to the Scriptures." Retargeted from a vague reference to "the Book of Concord's general confession of Christ's miracles" to the specific article that makes these claims.

reason: The Small Catechism's Table of Duties, retrieved in full, contains no content on divorce or remarriage at all — only household duty texts for husbands, wives, parents, children, servants and masters. No Book of Concord document was found addressing divorce with an exception clause.

fields.citation: Luther's Large Catechism, Lord's Prayer, the Sixth Petition
fields.note: The Large Catechism lists among the flesh's temptations "inchastity, laziness, gluttony and drunkenness, avarice and deception," naming drunkenness rather than drink itself as the vice. Retargeted from the Seventh Petition, which discusses deliverance from the devil generally and does not mention drink at all.

fields.citation: Augsburg Confession, Article XVI
fields.note: The Augsburg Confession says civil ordinances "are good works of God," and that the gospel "does not destroy the State or the family, but very much requires that they be preserved as ordinances of God."

fields.citation: Augsburg Confession, Article XVI
fields.note: The Augsburg Confession says it is right for Christians "to engage in just wars, to serve as soldiers," against those who forbid Christians from civil office.

fields.citation: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration, Article III; Small Catechism, The Sacrament of Holy Baptism
fields.note: The Solid Declaration says believers "are declared and regarded godly and righteous by faith" though "they still are and remain sinners to the grave," and the Small Catechism describes baptism's daily meaning: "the old Adam in us should, by daily contrition and repentance, be drowned and die... and a new man daily come forth and arise."

fields.citation: Augsburg Confession, Article XV
fields.note: The Augsburg Confession says usages "ought to be observed which may be observed without sin, and which are profitable unto tranquillity and good order," permitting a shared liturgical pattern without requiring one and without discussing a daily office or church calendar by name.

fields.citation: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration, Article XI
fields.note: The Solid Declaration says "God in His purpose has ordained before the time of the world by what crosses and sufferings He would conform every one of His elect to the image of His Son, and that to every one His cross shall and must work together for good."

fields.citation: Nicene Creed (Book of Concord, Ecumenical Creeds); Augsburg Confession, Article 1
fields.note: The Nicene Creed printed in the Book of Concord confesses the Son as "begotten of the Father before all worlds, God of God, Light of Light, very God of very God, begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father." Retargeted from Formula of Concord, Epitome 8, which speaks of Christ's person in the incarnation and only mentions eternal generation in passing.

sources.label: Retrieving Eternal Generation
sources.citation: Fred Sanders and Scott Swain, eds., 2017

fields.citation: Augsburg Confession, Article 1; Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration, Article VIII
fields.note: The Solid Declaration treats the Son's humiliation and exaltation as belonging to the incarnate state, saying the human nature's majesty was present already "when He was conceived in His mother's womb" though "laid aside... and kept it concealed in the state of His humiliation." It does not itself address an eternal ordering of authority between Father and Son; the shared, undivided will rests on the wider confession in Augsburg Confession, Article 1, that the three Persons are "of the same essence and power."

sources.label: The Rise and Fall of the Complementarian Doctrine of the Trinity

fields.citation: Augsburg Confession, Article 1
fields.note: The Augsburg Confession describes the one "Divine Essence... eternal, without body, without parts, of infinite power, wisdom, and goodness." The article affirms simplicity and eternity in these terms but does not use the word impassible.

fields.citation: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration, Article XI
fields.note: The Solid Declaration says "God sees and knows everything before it happens" and "foresees and foreknows everything that is or will be," whether good or bad.

reason: The Solid Declaration, Article I, defines the image of God as the "concreated hereditary righteousness in Paradise... truth, holiness, and righteousness" that was entirely and totally lost at the fall, not as reason, moral agency or an immortal soul wounded but surviving intact — the article separately notes that natural reason for "external things" persists, but does not equate that faculty with the divine image. This directly conflicts with the structural position's core claim that the image consists chiefly in capacities the fall "wounded but did not destroy."

fields.citation: Augsburg Confession, Article II
fields.note: The Augsburg Confession says original sin "is truly sin, even now condemning and bringing eternal death upon those not born again through Baptism and the Holy Ghost."

fields.citation: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration, Article II
fields.note: The Solid Declaration says that "in spiritual and divine things the intellect, heart, and will of the unregenerate man are utterly unable, by their own natural powers, to understand, believe, accept, think, will, begin, effect, do, work, or concur in working anything."

fields.citation: Luther's Small Catechism, explanation of the First Article of the Apostles' Creed
fields.note: The Small Catechism speaks of God as the one who has "given me my body and soul, eyes, ears, and all my limbs, my reason, and all my senses," naming body and soul rather than a separate soul and spirit. Retargeted from an uncited generalization about "standard Lutheran anthropology" to this specific text.

sources.label: Summa Theologiae
sources.citation: Thomas Aquinas, I q.75-76, on the unity of the soul

fields.citation: Augsburg Confession, Article XVII, "Of Christ's Return to Judgment"
fields.note: The Augsburg Confession says "at the Consummation of the World Christ will appear for judgment, and will raise up all the dead; He will give to the godly and elect eternal life and everlasting joys, but ungodly men and the devils He will condemn to be tormented without end."

sources.label: International Network of Churches, Declaration of Faith

fields.citation: Augsburg Confession, Article XVII
fields.note: The Augsburg Confession condemns "others who are now spreading certain Jewish opinions, that before the resurrection of the dead the godly shall take possession of the kingdom of the world, the ungodly being everywhere suppressed."

fields.citation: Augsburg Confession, Article XVII
fields.note: The Augsburg Confession frames Christ's return as a single event at "the Consummation of the World," when he judges and raises all the dead at once, without a separate prior gathering — an inference from its single-event eschatology rather than direct engagement with the modern pretribulational-rapture question.

fields.citation: Augsburg Confession, Article XVII
fields.note: The Augsburg Confession says ungodly men and devils will be condemned "to be tormented without end," and condemns "the Anabaptists, who think that there will be an end to the punishments of condemned men and devils."

fields.citation: Smalcald Articles (1537), Part II, Article 1, "The First and Chief Article"
fields.note: The Smalcald Articles say "there is none other name under heaven, given among men whereby we must be saved." Retargeted from Augsburg Confession, Article III-IV, which teach Christ's atonement and justification by faith but do not state the exclusivity claim this directly.

fields.citation: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration, Article XI
fields.note: The Solid Declaration says God "observes its order also in wicked acts or works, inasmuch as a limit and measure is fixed by God to the evil," while the "wicked, perverse will of the devil and of men" remains the cause of evil.

sources.label: Canons of Dordt
sources.citation: 1619, Third and Fourth Heads of Doctrine

fields.citation: Augsburg Confession, Article 9; Small Catechism, Part 4
fields.note: The Small Catechism says baptism "works forgiveness of sins, delivers from death and the devil, and gives eternal salvation to all who believe," and that it is not water alone but "the word of God which is in and with the water, and faith" that makes it effective.

reason: Formula of Concord, Epitome/Solid Declaration, Rule and Norm 1, retrieved in full, establishes Scripture as the sole standard by which doctrine is judged but nowhere identifies which books belong to the canon. No Book of Concord document naming the sixty-six books, or excluding the deuterocanonical books by name, was found.

Formula of Concord, Rule and Norm 1, retrieved in full, is about Scripture's supreme authority as the standard for judging doctrine, not about whether an ordinary reader can grasp what is necessary for salvation without a specially authorised interpreter — a different doctrine the document does not address. This is the same reused-catch-all citation the sample already caught misapplied to scripture.hermeneutic-method.

fields.citation: Augsburg Confession, Article I; Nicene Creed (Book of Concord, Ecumenical Creeds)
fields.note: The Augsburg Confession confesses God as "the Maker and Preserver of all things, visible and invisible," the traditional basis for affirming angels and demons as real created beings; neither text develops a separate treatment of them. Retargeted from a vague reference to "the three chief symbols" to the specific text that carries this language.
